pr_title: [Fix #13395] False positive for `Lint/UselessAssignment` when assigning in branch and block
pr_body:
As demonstrated in the issue #13395, there is a false positive as such:
```ruby
changed = false
^^^^^^^ Useless assignment to variable - `changed`.

if Random.rand > 1
  changed = true
end

[].each do
  changed = true
end

puts changed
```

In the presence of a conditional, the cop `Lint/UselessAssignment` can't be certain if the variable will be reassigned or not, so, very much like the case for blocks, the best approach is simply to ignore it.

There appears to be no benefit in actually looking into all branches and checking if all branches reassign since even then the outer assignment defines the variable.

This also applies to case statements.

-----------------

* [X] Feature branch is up-to-date with `master` (if not - rebase it).
* [X] Squashed related commits together.
* [X] Added tests.
* [X] Ran `bundle exec rake default`. It executes all tests and runs RuboCop on its own code.
* [X] Added an entry (file) to the [changelog folder](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/changelog/) named `{change_type}_{change_description}.md` if the new code introduces user-observable changes. See [changelog entry format](https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#changelog-entry-format) for details.

[1]: https://chris.beams.io/posts/git-commit/
pr_comments:
> There appears to be no benefit in actually looking into all branches and checking if all branches reassign since even then the outer assignment defines the variable.

I don't quite get this part, as by looking at them you can actually determine whether some assignment is void or not.

> > There appears to be no benefit in actually looking into all branches and checking if all branches reassign since even then the outer assignment defines the variable.
> 
> I don't quite get this part, as by looking at them you can actually determine whether some assignment is void or not.

Can you create an example? What I was trying to highlight is situations like this:

```ruby
changed = false

if Random.rand > 1
  changed = true
else 
  changed = false
end

[].each do
  changed = true
end

puts changed
```

Even considering that any branch will assign to `changed` the assignment above is not useless since it creates the variable. 
Out of the top of my head no examples come to mind that it matters to check all branches.

> Even considering that any branch will assign to changed the assignment above is not useless since it creates the variable.

So, your point applies only if there's a usage outside the branches, right? (in your case the `puts`)

> > Even considering that any branch will assign to changed the assignment above is not useless since it creates the variable.
> 
> So, your point applies only if there's a usage outside the branches, right? (in your case the `puts`)

I'd say so. And testing with, for instance:
```ruby
def some_method
  changed = false
  ^^^^^^^ Useless assignment to variable - `changed`.

  if Random.rand > 1
    changed = true
    ^^^^^^^ Useless assignment to variable - `changed`.
  else
    changed = false
    ^^^^^^^ Useless assignment to variable - `changed`.
  end
end
```

works as expected. However, one important detail, in the following scenario:

```ruby
def some_method
  changed = false

  if Random.rand > 1
    changed = true
  end

  [].each do
    changed = true
  end
end
```

the variable is not unused since it is captured by a block. This is respectful of the comments under `RuboCop::Cop::VariableForce::Variable::used?` that quote the following:

>         # This is a convenient way to check whether the variable is used
>        # in its entire variable lifetime.
>        # For more precise usage check, refer Assignment#used?.
>        #
>        # Once the variable is captured by a block, we have no idea
>        # when, where, and how many times the block would be invoked.
>        # This means we cannot track the usage of the variable.
>       # So we consider it's used to suppress false positive offenses.

@bbatsov
It's been a long time, I've kinda forgotten about this, sorry, where do we stand on this @bbatsov ?

issue_context.title: False positive for `Lint/UselessAssignment` when assigning in branch and block
issue_context.body:
## Expected behavior
The following code warns about a unused variable:

```rb
changed = false

if Random.rand > 1
  changed = true
end

[].each do
  changed = true
end

puts changed
```

I expect no offense for this case. The first assignment is meaningful, removing it will change the output from `false` to `nil`. Changed with https://github.com/rubocop/rubocop/pull/13389, not released yet.

## Actual behavior

```
$ bundle exec rubocop test.rb --only Lint/UselessAssignment
Inspecting 1 file
W

Offenses:

test.rb:1:1: W: [Correctable] Lint/UselessAssignment: Useless assignment to variable - changed.
changed = false
^^^^^^^

1 file inspected, 1 offense detected, 1 offense autocorrectable
```

## RuboCop version

```
Commit 8454d933
$ bundle exec rubocop -V
1.67.0 (using Parser 3.3.5.0, rubocop-ast 1.32.3, analyzing as Ruby 2.7, running on ruby 3.3.5) [x86_64-linux]
  - rubocop-performance 1.22.1
  - rubocop-rake 0.6.0
  - rubocop-rspec 3.2.0
```
comments:

```
def foo
  a = true # RuboCop: Useless assignment to variable - `a`. [Lint/UselessAssignment]
  if something
    a = false
  end
  [].each do |n|
    a = false
  end
  a
end
```
I'll take a look throughout the day if no one gets to it first

I've noticed a similar issue.  This code should produce no warnings:

```ruby
class Test
  attr_accessor :a

  def run
    a += 1 if condition_a
    a += 2 if condition_b
    a += 3 if condition_c
  end
end
```

however I get the `Lint/UselessAssignment` error for the final `if` condition.  More disturbing is what happens when I run `rubocop -a` on the file, it "corrects" to this:

```ruby
class Test
  attr_accessor :a

  def run
    a += 1 if condition_a
    a += 2 if condition_b
    a + 3 if condition_c    # WTF!?
  end
end
```
@opensourceame can you make a new issue for that? It seems to be something different since I get an offense even for earlier versions already.
Actually, I think that offense is correct. `a` in `run` doesn't reference your attribute, for that you would need to write it as `self.a`

Here's a minimal example of this false positive that I ran into today:

```ruby
def my_method
  state = true

  # This false could be a conditional that returns false
  if false
    state = false
  end

  # This empty array could have been a query that returned no results, for example
  [].each do
    state = false
  end

  # We want to return the boolean, which defaults to true at the top
  state
end
```

This is clearly silly code, but Rubocop reports:

```
rubocop ".../scratches/scratch_14.rb" --only Lint/UselessAssignment
W

Offenses:

.../scratches/scratch_14.rb:2:3: W: [Correctable] Lint/UselessAssignment: Useless assignment to variable - state.
  state = true
  ^^^^^

1 file inspected, 1 offense detected, 1 offense autocorrectable

```

Running that method without `state = true` at the top will cause the method to return `nil` instead of `true`.
